evidence.note: Opens with the thesis that a shared array could undercut daytime power costs and previews a 12-month pilot on two roofs.
Problem: about 40% of flats' electricity spend falls in daylight hours; big stat £612 median yearly spend per flat. No figure for what the array would save a flat or the co-op.

Kicker says 'Problem' but the title reports 26 of 33 households support a pilot, which is demand or support evidence rather than problem or stakes; a resident quote about paying peak rates gives a human angle.
Resolution: 12-month pilot on blocks C and D, 64 kW, £86,400, Install → 12 months measured → Go or stop review.
Mechanism comes after the pilot plan: array → landlord supply → flats monthly credit; insight that heavy daytime users get the largest credit.
Risks: roof leaks, falling tariffs and upkeep, plus disputed payback (installer 7 years, treasurer 11 years).
Closes with a clear ask: approve the £86,400 pilot with a go or stop review at twelve months.

rationale: The deck has a problem (daytime spend), a resolution (pilot and mechanism), risks and a clear final ask. But the stakes are thin: no saving per flat or for the co-op is ever stated, so the case for £86,400 rests on payback figures shown only under risks. The order also weakens the case: a survey-support slide is labelled as problem, and the pilot plan comes before the mechanism. That fits level 3.
